topic: Governing Actions in organisations and enterprises

notes.front: What is an Actions policy?
notes.back: A setting that governs how GitHub Actions workflows run, configured in the Policies section of the Actions settings.
notes.explanation: Actions policies sit apart from the General settings and exist at enterprise, organisation and repository level.
notes.example: Like house rules set by a building’s management: every flat follows them, whatever an individual tenant would prefer.
notes.source: GitHub Docs, “About Actions policies”, “About Actions policies”
notes.evidence: Actions policies let you govern how GitHub Actions workflows run. You can configure them in the **Policies** section of your GitHub Actions settings (separate from the **General** settings). Actions policies are available at the enterprise, organization, and repository levels.

notes.front: In an organisation’s Actions permissions, what is the allow list?
notes.back: The list of specified actions and reusable workflows (or whole organisations and repositories) that workflows may use.
notes.explanation: Entries can name single actions and reusable workflows, or whole organisations and repositories.
notes.example: Like a guest list at a door: only names on it get in, and some names can be struck through to keep them out.
notes.source: GitHub Docs, “Disabling or limiting GitHub Actions for your organization”, “Allowing select actions and reusable workflows to run”
notes.evidence: You can restrict workflows to use actions and reusable workflows in specific organizations and repositories.

notes.front: What is a workflow execution protection?
notes.back: An Actions policy that defines an allowlist of who can trigger workflows and which events may run them.
notes.explanation: It is currently the only type of Actions policy; GitHub plans to add more over time.
notes.example: Like a building’s access badge system: it decides which people may start the lift and at which doors.
notes.source: GitHub Docs, “About Actions policies”, “About workflow execution protections”
notes.evidence: They currently contain one type of policy: workflow execution protections. GitHub plans to add more policies over time. ## About workflow execution protections With workflow execution protections, you can define an allowlist that controls who can trigger GitHub Actions workflows and which events are permitted to run them.

notes.front: What does an actor rule control?
notes.back: Who can trigger workflows, such as individual users, repository roles or GitHub Apps.
notes.explanation: By default anyone with write access can trigger workflows; an actor rule separates contributing code from running CI.
notes.example: Like letting a visitor into the office but not giving them the key to the server room.
notes.source: GitHub Docs, “About Actions policies”, “Available rules”
notes.evidence: Actor rules control who can trigger workflows, including individual users, repository roles, GitHub Apps, Copilot, and Dependabot. By default, every user with write access to a repository can trigger workflows. Actor rules let you separate who contributes code from who runs your CI

notes.front: What does an event rule control?
notes.back: Which events are permitted to trigger workflows, such as `push` or `pull_request_target`.
notes.explanation: It is the second rule type in workflow execution protections, beside actor rules; GitHub plans to add more rules.
notes.example: Like a shop that opens only for certain kinds of delivery, whoever is driving the van.
notes.source: GitHub Docs, “About Actions policies”, “Available rules”
notes.evidence: Event rules control which events are permitted, such as `push`, `pull_request`, `pull_request_target`, and `workflow_dispatch`. GitHub plans to add more rules over time.

notes.front: For fork pull request approvals, who is a first-time contributor?
notes.back: A user who has never had a commit or pull request merged into the repository.
notes.explanation: The setting of the same name holds such users’ workflows for approval; once a change of theirs is merged, it no longer does.
notes.example: Like a new library member who must show ID at the desk until their first loan has been returned.
notes.source: GitHub Docs, “Disabling or limiting GitHub Actions for your organization”, “Configuring required approval for workflows from public forks”
notes.evidence: Require approval for first-time contributors**. Only users who have never had a commit or pull request merged into this repository will require approval to run workflows.

notes.front: By default, GitHub Actions is {{c1::enabled}} on all repositories and organisations.
notes.back: enabled
notes.explanation: Owners can then disable it, or limit it to actions and reusable workflows in their organisation.
notes.source: GitHub Docs, “Disabling or limiting GitHub Actions for your organization”, “About GitHub Actions permissions for your organization”
notes.evidence: By default, GitHub Actions is enabled on all repositories and organizations. You can choose to disable GitHub Actions or limit it to actions and reusable workflows in your organization.

notes.front: A repository owner disables GitHub Actions for the repository but leaves its workflow files in place. What runs?
notes.back: Nothing: when Actions is disabled, no workflows run in the repository.
notes.explanation: Disabling is all-or-nothing; limiting which actions run is the finer alternative.
notes.source: GitHub Docs, “Disabling or limiting GitHub Actions for your organization”, “About GitHub Actions permissions for your organization”
notes.evidence: You can disable GitHub Actions for all repositories in your organization. When you disable GitHub Actions, no workflows run in your repository.

notes.front: What two things can an organisation’s GitHub Actions permissions restrict?
notes.back: Which repositories may run Actions, and whether public actions and reusable workflows may be used.
notes.explanation: Owners can allow all repositories, only specific ones or none, and can confine workflows to local actions.
notes.source: GitHub Docs, “Disabling or limiting GitHub Actions for your organization”, “Managing GitHub Actions permissions for your organization”
notes.evidence: You can choose to disable GitHub Actions for all repositories in your organization, or only allow specific repositories. You can also limit the use of public actions and reusable workflows, so that people can only use local actions and reusable workflows that exist in your organization.

notes.front: You script an organisation so that only a chosen set of its repositories can run Actions. Which value do you give `enabled_repositories`?
notes.back: `selected` (the other values are `all` and `none`).
notes.explanation: This body parameter sets which of the organisation’s repositories are allowed to run GitHub Actions.
notes.source: GitHub Docs, “REST API endpoints for GitHub Actions permissions”, “Set GitHub Actions permissions for an organization”
notes.evidence: The policy that controls the repositories in the organization that are allowed to run GitHub Actions. Can be one of: `all`, `none`, `selected`

notes.front: Through the permissions endpoint, what values can `allowed_actions` take for an organisation?
notes.back: `all`, `local_only` or `selected`.
notes.explanation: This body parameter sets which actions and reusable workflows are allowed to run.
notes.source: GitHub Docs, “REST API endpoints for GitHub Actions permissions”, “Set GitHub Actions permissions for an organization”
notes.evidence: The permissions policy that controls the actions and reusable workflows that are allowed to run. Can be one of: `all`, `local_only`, `selected`

notes.front: An organisation allows only actions and reusable workflows from within itself. Can its workflows use `actions/checkout`?
notes.back: No. That policy blocks all access to actions authored by GitHub.
notes.explanation: `actions/checkout` is the docs’ own example of an action that would not be accessible.
notes.source: GitHub Docs, “Disabling or limiting GitHub Actions for your organization”, “Managing GitHub Actions permissions for your organization”
notes.evidence: When you allow actions and reusable workflows from only in your organization, the policy blocks all access to actions authored by GitHub. For example, the [`actions/checkout`](https://github.com/actions/checkout) action would not be accessible.

notes.front: An owner changes the policy to allow only the organisation’s own actions. Next morning every workflow fails at its `actions/checkout` step. What happened?
notes.choices:
A) The policy blocks actions authored by GitHub
B) The workflows need approval from a maintainer
C) Checkout now needs a full-length commit SHA
D) `actions/checkout` must be on the allow list as `actions/*@*`
notes.back: A) The policy blocks actions authored by GitHub
notes.choicesExplained: C: SHA pinning is a separate option, not part of this change. B: approval applies to fork pull requests. D: the organisation-only option has no allow list; that belongs to the option that also selects outside actions.
notes.explanation: Organisation-only means exactly that: even GitHub’s own actions are shut out.
notes.source: GitHub Docs, “Disabling or limiting GitHub Actions for your organization”, “Managing GitHub Actions permissions for your organization”
notes.evidence: When you allow actions and reusable workflows from only in your organization, the policy blocks all access to actions authored by GitHub.

notes.front: Under “Allow owner, and select non-owner, actions and reusable workflows”, are local actions still allowed?
notes.back: Yes. Local actions (`./` and `$/`) and reusable workflows are allowed, with extra options for others.
notes.explanation: This option starts from what is inside the organisation and then lets you add chosen outside actions.
notes.source: GitHub Docs, “Disabling or limiting GitHub Actions for your organization”, “Allowing select actions and reusable workflows to run”
notes.evidence: local actions (`./` and `$/`) and reusable workflows are allowed, and there are additional options for allowing other specific actions and reusable workflows

notes.front: An organisation wants its workflows to use every action in the `actions` and `github` organisations without listing each one. Which option does it tick?
notes.back: “Allow actions created by GitHub”.
notes.explanation: Actions created by GitHub live in those two organisations, and this option admits all of them.
notes.source: GitHub Docs, “Disabling or limiting GitHub Actions for your organization”, “Allowing select actions and reusable workflows to run”
notes.evidence: You can allow all actions created by GitHub to be used by workflows. Actions created by GitHub are located in the `actions` and `github` organizations.

notes.front: What does “Allow Marketplace actions by verified creators” permit?
notes.back: All GitHub Marketplace actions whose creator GitHub has verified as a partner organisation.
notes.explanation: The creator must be one that GitHub has verified as a partner organisation.
notes.source: GitHub Docs, “Disabling or limiting GitHub Actions for your organization”, “Allowing select actions and reusable workflows to run”
notes.evidence: You can allow all GitHub Marketplace actions created by verified creators to be used by workflows. When GitHub has verified the creator of the action as a partner organization,

notes.front: Specified actions in the allow list cannot be set to more than {{c1::1000}}.
notes.explanation: The cap counts the actions you specify in the list.
notes.source: GitHub Docs, “Disabling or limiting GitHub Actions for your organization”, “Allowing select actions and reusable workflows to run”
notes.evidence: You can restrict workflows to use actions and reusable workflows in specific organizations and repositories. Specified actions cannot be set to more than 1000.

notes.front: In the allow list, an action is written as {{c1::`OWNER/REPOSITORY@TAG-OR-SHA`}}.
notes.back: `OWNER/REPOSITORY@TAG-OR-SHA`
notes.explanation: It is the same syntax a workflow uses to select the action, so you can pin to a tag or a SHA.
notes.source: GitHub Docs, “Disabling or limiting GitHub Actions for your organization”, “Allowing select actions and reusable workflows to run”
notes.evidence: To restrict access to specific tags or commit SHAs of an action or reusable workflow, use the same syntax used in the workflow to select the action or reusable workflow. * For an action, the syntax is `OWNER/REPOSITORY@TAG-OR-SHA`.

notes.front: How is a reusable workflow written in the allow list?
notes.back: `OWNER/REPOSITORY/PATH/FILENAME@TAG-OR-SHA`
notes.explanation: Unlike an action, a reusable workflow entry names the path and file inside the repository.
notes.source: GitHub Docs, “Disabling or limiting GitHub Actions for your organization”, “Allowing select actions and reusable workflows to run”
notes.evidence: For a reusable workflow, the syntax is `OWNER/REPOSITORY/PATH/FILENAME@TAG-OR-SHA`. For example, `octo-org/another-repo/.github/workflows/workflow.yml@v1`.

notes.front: Which character matches patterns in the allow list?
notes.back: The `*` wildcard, as in `space-org*/*` for every organisation whose name starts with `space-org`.
notes.explanation: A wildcard lets one entry cover whole organisations or families of repositories.
notes.source: GitHub Docs, “Disabling or limiting GitHub Actions for your organization”, “Allowing select actions and reusable workflows to run”
notes.evidence: You can use the `*` wildcard character to match patterns. For example, to allow all actions and reusable workflows in organizations that start with `space-org`, you can specify `space-org*/*`.

notes.front: How do you block a pattern in the allow list?
notes.back: Put `!` in front of it, as in `!space-org/action@*`.
notes.explanation: Blocking entries carve exceptions out of broader allowing patterns in the same list.
notes.source: GitHub Docs, “Disabling or limiting GitHub Actions for your organization”, “Allowing select actions and reusable workflows to run”
notes.evidence: Use the `!` prefix to block patterns. For example, to allow all actions and reusable workflows from the `space-org` organization, but block a specific action like `space-org/action`, you can specify `space-org/*, !space-org/action@*`.

notes.front: By default, only actions and reusable workflows {{c1::specified in the list}} are allowed.
notes.back: specified in the list
notes.explanation: To allow everything except a few, the list must start with `*` and then add the blocks.
notes.source: GitHub Docs, “Disabling or limiting GitHub Actions for your organization”, “Allowing select actions and reusable workflows to run”
notes.evidence: By default, only actions and reusable workflows specified in the list will be allowed. To allow all actions and reusable workflows while also blocking specific actions, you can specify `*, !space-org/action@*`.

notes.front: Security wants every action allowed except `acme/risky-action` in all its versions. What do you put in the allow list?
notes.back: C) `*, !acme/risky-action@*`
notes.choicesExplained: A: this allows only the `acme` organisation. B: with no allowing pattern, nothing listed is allowed. D: this allows everything and blocks nothing.
notes.explanation: Only listed items are allowed by default, so the list needs `*` before the blocking entry.
notes.source: GitHub Docs, “Disabling or limiting GitHub Actions for your organization”, “Allowing select actions and reusable workflows to run”
notes.evidence: By default, only actions and reusable workflows specified in the list will be allowed. To allow all actions and reusable workflows while also blocking specific actions, you can specify `*, !space-org/action@*`.

notes.front: With “Require actions to be pinned to a full-length commit SHA” on, {{c1::reusable workflows}} can still be referenced by tag.
notes.back: reusable workflows
notes.explanation: The requirement covers actions only, so reusable workflow references are unaffected.
notes.source: GitHub Docs, “Disabling or limiting GitHub Actions for your organization”, “Managing GitHub Actions permissions for your organization”
notes.evidence: When you enable **Require actions to be pinned to a full-length commit SHA**, all actions must be pinned to a full-length commit SHA to be used. This includes actions from your organization and actions authored by GitHub. Reusable workflows can still be referenced by tag.

notes.front: Your organisation has just switched on the full-length SHA pinning requirement. Which reference will still work unchanged?
notes.choices:
A) `uses: actions/checkout@v6`
B) `uses: my-org/pipelines/.github/workflows/ci.yml@v2`
C) `uses: actions/setup-node@v7`
D) `uses: my-org/lint-action@main`
notes.back: B) `uses: my-org/pipelines/.github/workflows/ci.yml@v2`
notes.choicesExplained: A and C: GitHub-authored actions must be pinned to a SHA too. D: your own organisation’s actions are also covered, and `main` is a branch, not a SHA.
notes.explanation: B calls a reusable workflow, and reusable workflows can still be referenced by tag.
notes.source: GitHub Docs, “Disabling or limiting GitHub Actions for your organization”, “Managing GitHub Actions permissions for your organization”
notes.evidence: This includes actions from your organization and actions authored by GitHub. Reusable workflows can still be referenced by tag.

notes.front: Which body parameter of `PUT /orgs/{org}/actions/permissions` sets whether actions must be pinned to a full-length SHA?
notes.back: `sha_pinning_required`, a boolean.
notes.explanation: Setting it to true requires every action to be pinned to a full-length SHA.
notes.source: GitHub Docs, “REST API endpoints for GitHub Actions permissions”, “Set GitHub Actions permissions for an organization”
notes.evidence: `sha_pinning_required`** (boolean) Whether actions must be pinned to a full-length commit SHA.

notes.front: If an enterprise enforces no Actions policies, who controls GitHub Actions for its organisations?
notes.back: Organisation owners and users with the “Manage organization Actions policies” permission.
notes.explanation: Enterprise policies narrow the options open to those people; without them, they have full control.
notes.source: GitHub Docs, “Enforcing policies for GitHub Actions in your enterprise”, “What are policies for GitHub Actions?”
notes.evidence: Enterprise policies control the options that are available to enterprise members when they use GitHub Actions. If you don't enforce enterprise policies, organization owners and users with the "Manage organization Actions policies" permission have full control over GitHub Actions for their organizations.

notes.front: Why might an organisation owner be unable to change the organisation’s GitHub Actions permissions?
notes.back: The organisation may be managed by an enterprise that has an overriding policy.
notes.explanation: An enterprise policy sits above the organisation and can lock the settings beneath it.
notes.source: GitHub Docs, “Disabling or limiting GitHub Actions for your organization”, “Managing GitHub Actions permissions for your organization”
notes.evidence: You might not be able to manage these settings if your organization is managed by an enterprise that has overriding policy.

notes.front: What three options does an enterprise have for which of its organisations can use GitHub Actions?
notes.back: Enable for all organisations; enable for specific organisations; disable for all organisations.
notes.explanation: This is the first choice on the enterprise Policies page, before the rules about which actions may run.
notes.source: GitHub Docs, “Enforcing policies for GitHub Actions in your enterprise”, “Policies”
notes.evidence: In the "Policies" section, you can control which organizations within your enterprise can use GitHub Actions, with the following options: * Enable GitHub Actions for all organizations * Enable GitHub Actions for specific organizations * Disable GitHub Actions for all organizations

notes.front: An enterprise enables GitHub Actions only for specific organisations. What happens to code scanning in the organisations left out?
notes.back: They are blocked from using code scanning and GitHub Code Quality analysis.
notes.explanation: Not enabling Actions for an organisation has the same effect as disabling it there.
notes.source: GitHub Docs, “Enforcing policies for GitHub Actions in your enterprise”, “Policies”
notes.evidence: If you disable GitHub Actions, or do not enable the feature for one or more organizations, this blocks affected organizations from using code scanning and GitHub Code Quality analysis.

notes.front: Which enterprise option permits only actions and reusable workflows defined in the enterprise’s own repositories?
notes.back: “Allow enterprise actions and reusable workflows”.
notes.explanation: Like the organisation-only option, it also blocks actions authored by GitHub, such as `actions/checkout`.
notes.source: GitHub Docs, “Enforcing policies for GitHub Actions in your enterprise”, “Controlling access to public actions and reusable workflows”
notes.evidence: Allow enterprise actions and reusable workflows:** Only actions and reusable workflows defined in a repository within the enterprise can be used. Blocks all access to actions authored by GitHub, such as the [`actions/checkout`](https://github.com/actions/checkout) action.

notes.front: What does “Allow enterprise, and select non-enterprise, actions and reusable workflows” permit?
notes.back: Anything defined in the enterprise’s repositories, plus any action or reusable workflow matching criteria you specify.
notes.explanation: It widens the enterprise-only option with outside actions that match your criteria.
notes.source: GitHub Docs, “Enforcing policies for GitHub Actions in your enterprise”, “Controlling access to public actions and reusable workflows”
notes.evidence: Any action or reusable workflow defined in a repository within the enterprise can be used, plus any action or reusable workflow that matches criteria you specify.

notes.front: An enterprise allows only enterprise actions. A step says `uses: ./.github/actions/setup`. Is that step blocked?
notes.back: No. Policies never restrict local actions on the runner filesystem.
notes.explanation: A `uses:` path starting with `./` points at an action already on the runner.
notes.source: GitHub Docs, “Enforcing policies for GitHub Actions in your enterprise”, “Allow enterprise, and select non-enterprise, actions and reusable workflows”
notes.evidence: Policies never restrict access to local actions on the runner filesystem (where the `uses:` path start with `./`).

notes.front: What are two attack patterns that workflow execution protections can disrupt?
notes.back: Poisoned pipeline execution from pull requests, and manual-trigger abuse.
notes.explanation: The docs also list untrusted-actor execution and exploitation of a misconfigured workflow file.
notes.source: GitHub Docs, “About Actions policies”, “About workflow execution protections”
notes.evidence: * **Poisoned pipeline execution from pull requests.** Restrict or prohibit `pull_request_target`, including in public repositories where it is most often exploited. * **Manual-trigger abuse.** Limit `workflow_dispatch` so untrusted identities cannot start workflows. * **Untrusted-actor execution.** Block low-trust identities from triggering workflows entirely. * **Misconfiguration exploitation.**

notes.front: When workflow execution protections are enforced, a disallowed workflow run {{c1::fails with an error}}.
notes.back: fails with an error
notes.explanation: The error names the event that was not allowed and the workflow file.
notes.source: GitHub Docs, “About Actions policies”, “About workflow execution protections”
notes.evidence: When enforced, disallowed workflow runs will fail with an error. For example: ```text Event 'workflow_dispatch' is not allowed to trigger Actions workflows. Workflow file: '.github/workflows/0-welcome.yml'.

notes.front: With no actor rules, who can trigger workflows in a repository?
notes.back: Every user with write access to it.
notes.explanation: Actor rules exist to narrow this default.
notes.source: GitHub Docs, “About Actions policies”, “Available rules”
notes.evidence: By default, every user with write access to a repository can trigger workflows.

notes.front: A contractor needs write access to push branches, but must not be able to run your CI workflows. What do you configure?
notes.choices:
A) A branch protection rule
B) An event rule that blocks `push`
C) Approval for first-time contributors
D) An actor rule
notes.back: D) An actor rule
notes.choicesExplained: B: blocking `push` would stop everyone’s push workflows. C: that applies to fork pull requests, not to a collaborator with write access. A: it protects branches, not who may run workflows.
notes.explanation: Actor rules let you grant write access without granting the ability to execute workflows.
notes.source: GitHub Docs, “About Actions policies”, “Available rules”
notes.evidence: Actor rules let you separate who contributes code from who runs your CI, so you can grant a contributor write access without granting them the ability to execute workflows.

notes.front: After a workflow was started by hand by an unexpected account, you want to limit manual starts across the organisation, whatever the workflow files say. What fits best?
notes.choices:
A) Remove `workflow_dispatch` from every workflow file
B) An event rule that limits `workflow_dispatch`
C) Allow only the organisation’s own actions
D) Require approval for all external contributors
notes.back: B) An event rule that limits `workflow_dispatch`
notes.choicesExplained: A: editing files one by one is what a central policy avoids, and a file could add it back. D: that governs fork pull requests. C: that limits which actions run, not which events trigger.
notes.explanation: Event rules decide which events may trigger workflows, and limiting `workflow_dispatch` stops untrusted identities starting workflows.
notes.source: GitHub Docs, “About Actions policies”, “About workflow execution protections”
notes.evidence: Manual-trigger abuse.** Limit `workflow_dispatch` so untrusted identities cannot start workflows.

notes.front: A public repository relies on a `pull_request_target` workflow. What does GitHub’s new default policy do to it, and from when?
notes.back: It blocks the `pull_request_target` event in public repositories, enforced from 2 November 2026.
notes.explanation: GitHub added it as a default, so it applies without any setting of your own.
notes.source: GitHub Docs, “About Actions policies”, “About workflow execution protections”
notes.evidence: GitHub has added a default policy that will block the `pull_request_target` event in public repositories. This policy will be enforced on November 2, 2026.

notes.front: Why do workflows on pull requests from some outside contributors to public repositories not run automatically?
notes.back: They may need approval first, because fork workflows can be modified for abusive purposes.
notes.explanation: Fork workflows have no secrets, but abusive changes can still be a nuisance for maintainers.
notes.source: GitHub Docs, “Disabling or limiting GitHub Actions for your organization”, “Configuring required approval for workflows from public forks”
notes.evidence: Although workflows from forks do not have access to sensitive data such as secrets, they can be an annoyance for maintainers if they are modified for abusive purposes. To help prevent this, workflows on pull requests to public repositories from some outside contributors will not run automatically, and might need to be approved first.

notes.front: When GitHub decides whether a fork pull request workflow needs approval, whose identity does it check?
notes.back: Both the pull request’s author and the actor of the event that triggers the workflow.
notes.explanation: Approval is needed if either of them is someone the chosen policy covers.
notes.source: GitHub Docs, “Disabling or limiting GitHub Actions for your organization”, “Configuring required approval for workflows from public forks”
notes.evidence: Both the pull request author and the actor of the pull request event triggering the workflow will be checked to determine if approval is required.

notes.front: By default, all {{c1::first-time contributors}} require approval to run workflows.
notes.back: first-time contributors
notes.explanation: It is the default, before any owner changes the setting.
notes.source: GitHub Docs, “Disabling or limiting GitHub Actions for your organization”, “Configuring required approval for workflows from public forks”
notes.evidence: By default, all first-time contributors require approval to run workflows.

notes.front: Which fork-approval setting covers only users who are new on GitHub and have never had a change merged into the repository?
notes.back: “Require approval for first-time contributors who are new to GitHub”.
notes.explanation: Both conditions must hold, so it is the narrowest of the three settings.
notes.source: GitHub Docs, “Disabling or limiting GitHub Actions for your organization”, “Configuring required approval for workflows from public forks”
notes.evidence: Require approval for first-time contributors who are new to GitHub**. Only users who are both new on GitHub and who have never had a commit or pull request merged into this repository will require approval to run workflows.

notes.front: Which fork-approval setting covers every user who is neither a member or owner of the repository nor a member of the organisation?
notes.back: “Require approval for all external contributors”.
notes.explanation: It ignores merge history, so it is the strictest of the three settings.
notes.source: GitHub Docs, “Disabling or limiting GitHub Actions for your organization”, “Configuring required approval for workflows from public forks”
notes.evidence: Require approval for all external contributors** All users that are not a member or owner of this repository and not a member of the organization will require approval to run workflows.

notes.front: How could a malicious user get past a policy that requires approval only for first-time contributors?
notes.back: By first getting a small, harmless change, such as a typo fix, merged into the repository.
notes.explanation: After any merged commit or pull request, the user no longer needs approval under those settings.
notes.source: GitHub Docs, “Disabling or limiting GitHub Actions for your organization”, “Configuring required approval for workflows from public forks”
notes.evidence: a user that has had any commit or pull request merged into the repository will not require approval. A malicious user could meet this requirement by getting a simple typo or other innocuous change accepted by a maintainer

notes.front: A first-time contributor opens a fork pull request. The repository also has a `pull_request_target` workflow. Does that workflow wait for approval?
notes.back: No. It runs in the base branch’s context, which is trusted, so it always runs.
notes.explanation: Approval settings cover fork code; `pull_request_target` runs the base branch’s workflow instead.
notes.source: GitHub Docs, “Disabling or limiting GitHub Actions for your organization”, “Configuring required approval for workflows from public forks”
notes.evidence: Workflows triggered by `pull_request_target` events are run in the context of the base branch. Since the base branch is considered trusted, workflows triggered by these events will always run, regardless of approval settings.

notes.front: A public project wants every pull request workflow from anyone outside the organisation held until a maintainer approves it, however many changes that person has had merged. Which setting?
notes.choices:
A) Require approval for first-time contributors
B) Require approval for first-time contributors who are new to GitHub
C) An actor rule allowing only repository admins
D) Require approval for all external contributors
notes.back: D) Require approval for all external contributors
notes.choicesExplained: A and B: a user with any merged change no longer needs approval under these. C: actor rules decide who may trigger workflows, not approval of fork pull requests.
notes.explanation: Only the external-contributors setting ignores merge history and covers everyone outside the organisation.
notes.source: GitHub Docs, “Disabling or limiting GitHub Actions for your organization”, “Configuring required approval for workflows from public forks”
notes.evidence: All users that are not a member or owner of this repository and not a member of the organization will require approval to run workflows.

notes.front: On your own runners, does a fork-approval policy stop malicious pull request code from running?
notes.back: No. Code from users allowed to bypass approval, or from approved pull requests, runs automatically.
notes.explanation: Both a user allowed to bypass approval and an approved pull request lead to the code running automatically.
notes.source: GitHub Docs, “Disabling or limiting GitHub Actions for your organization”, “Configuring required approval for workflows from public forks”
notes.evidence: If you are using self-hosted runners, potentially malicious user-controlled workflow code will execute automatically if the user is allowed to bypass approval in the set approval policy or if the pull request is approved.

notes.front: For forks of private repositories, what does “Run workflows from fork pull requests” give those workflows?
notes.back: A read-only `GITHUB_TOKEN` and no access to secrets.
notes.explanation: Such workflows run without secrets and cannot write with the token.
notes.source: GitHub Docs, “Disabling or limiting GitHub Actions for your organization”, “Enabling workflows for private repository forks”
notes.evidence: Run workflows from fork pull requests** - Allows users to run workflows from fork pull requests, using a `GITHUB_TOKEN` with read-only permission, and with no access to secrets.

notes.front: If an organisation disables a private-fork workflow policy, can one of its repositories enable it?
notes.back: No. But a policy the organisation enables can be disabled for individual repositories.
notes.explanation: The organisation sets the ceiling and repositories may only tighten below it.
notes.source: GitHub Docs, “Disabling or limiting GitHub Actions for your organization”, “Enabling workflows for private repository forks”
notes.evidence: If a policy is disabled for an organization, it cannot be enabled for repositories. If an organization enables a policy, the policy can be disabled for individual repositories.

notes.front: What happens to a repository’s existing own runners when an organisation disables repository-level runners you host yourself?
notes.back: They are listed as “Disabled” and get no new workflow jobs.
notes.explanation: They stay listed, but receive no further work.
notes.source: GitHub Docs, “Disabling or limiting GitHub Actions for your organization”, “Limiting the use of self-hosted runners”
notes.evidence: If a repository already has self-hosted runners when you disable their use, these will be listed with the status "Disabled" and they will not be assigned any new workflow jobs.

notes.front: What does disabling standard GitHub-provided runners for an organisation require of its workflows?
notes.back: They must target runners through runner groups.
notes.explanation: This helps enforce consistent access controls and governance.
notes.source: GitHub Docs, “Disabling or limiting GitHub Actions for your organization”, “Disabling standard hosted runners”
notes.evidence: You can disable standard GitHub-hosted runners at the organization level. This setting requires workflows to target runners through runner groups and helps enforce consistent access controls and governance.

notes.front: In a newly created organisation, what access does `GITHUB_TOKEN` have by default?
notes.back: Read access only, for the `contents` and `packages` scopes.
notes.explanation: The token can read these scopes but not write to them, so a job that needs to write must be given more access, for example with the `permissions` key.
notes.source: GitHub Docs, “Disabling or limiting GitHub Actions for your organization”, “Configuring the default GITHUB_TOKEN permissions”
notes.evidence: By default, when you create a new organization, `GITHUB_TOKEN` only has read access for the `contents` and `packages` scopes.

notes.front: An organisation chooses the restrictive default for `GITHUB_TOKEN`. What happens in its repositories’ settings?
notes.back: The same option is selected there, and the permissive option is disabled.
notes.explanation: Repositories cannot loosen a restrictive default set above them.
notes.source: GitHub Docs, “Disabling or limiting GitHub Actions for your organization”, “Setting the permissions of the GITHUB_TOKEN for your organization”
notes.evidence: If you select a restrictive option as the default in your organization settings, the same option is selected in the settings for repositories within your organization, and the permissive option is disabled.

notes.front: In a newly created organisation, a workflow that tries to approve a pull request is refused. Why?
notes.back: By default, workflows in a new organisation are not allowed to create or approve pull requests.
notes.explanation: Owners can choose to allow it, but it starts switched off.
notes.source: GitHub Docs, “Disabling or limiting GitHub Actions for your organization”, “Preventing GitHub Actions from creating or approving pull requests”
notes.evidence: You can choose to allow or prevent GitHub Actions workflows from creating or approving pull requests. By default, when you create a new organization, workflows are not allowed to create or approve pull requests.

notes.front: A team has never touched its retention settings. How long are its workflow runs, artifacts and logs kept?
notes.back: 90 days, after which they are deleted automatically.
notes.explanation: That is the default retention period for checks, runs, statuses, artifacts and logs.
notes.source: GitHub Docs, “Configuring the retention period for checks, workflow runs, commit statuses, artifacts, and logs in your organization”, “Configuring the retention period for checks, workflow runs, commit statuses, artifacts, and logs in your organization”
notes.evidence: By default, checks, workflow runs, commit statuses, and the artifacts and log files generated by workflows are retained for 90 days before they are automatically deleted.

notes.front: What retention period can you set for a public repository?
notes.back: Anywhere from 1 to 90 days.
notes.explanation: Public repositories cannot go above the 90-day default.
notes.source: GitHub Docs, “Configuring the retention period for checks, workflow runs, commit statuses, artifacts, and logs in your organization”, “Configuring the retention period for checks, workflow runs, commit statuses, artifacts, and logs in your organization”
notes.evidence: For public repositories: you can change this retention period to anywhere between 1 day or 90 days.

notes.front: What retention period can you set for a private repository?
notes.back: Anywhere from 1 to 400 days.
notes.explanation: Private repositories may keep data far longer than public ones.
notes.source: GitHub Docs, “Configuring the retention period for checks, workflow runs, commit statuses, artifacts, and logs in your organization”, “Configuring the retention period for checks, workflow runs, commit statuses, artifacts, and logs in your organization”
notes.evidence: For private repositories: you can change this retention period to anywhere between 1 day or 400 days.

notes.front: You shorten the retention period. Does it apply to artifacts and logs that already exist?
notes.back: No. It applies only to new objects.
notes.explanation: Existing objects keep the period that applied when they were created.
notes.source: GitHub Docs, “Configuring the retention period for checks, workflow runs, commit statuses, artifacts, and logs in your organization”, “Configuring the retention period for checks, workflow runs, commit statuses, artifacts, and logs in your organization”
notes.evidence: When you customize the retention period, it only applies to new checks, workflow runs, commit statuses, artifacts, and log files, and does not retroactively apply to existing objects.

notes.front: An organisation set retention to 30 days last year, yet in September 2026 its year-old workflow runs are still listed. Why?
notes.back: Until 1 October 2026, checks, workflow runs and commit statuses are kept 400+ days whatever the setting.
notes.explanation: From 1 October 2026 the retention setting covers them as well as artifacts and logs.
notes.source: GitHub Docs, “Configuring the retention period for checks, workflow runs, commit statuses, artifacts, and logs in your organization”, “Configuring the retention period for checks, workflow runs, commit statuses, artifacts, and logs in your organization”
notes.evidence: Starting October 1, 2026, these policies will apply to checks, workflow runs, and commit statuses in addition to artifacts and logs. Until then, checks, workflow runs, and commit statuses are retained for 400+ days regardless of your configured retention period.

notes.front: Do retention policies cover commit statuses created by third-party integrations?
notes.back: Yes. The policies are not limited to data created by GitHub Actions.
notes.explanation: They apply to check suites, check runs and commit statuses, whoever created them.
notes.source: GitHub Docs, “Configuring the retention period for checks, workflow runs, commit statuses, artifacts, and logs in your organization”, “Configuring the retention period for checks, workflow runs, commit statuses, artifacts, and logs in your organization”
notes.evidence: These retention policies apply to checks data, including check suites and check runs, and to commit statuses, including those created by third-party integrations. The policies are not limited to data created by GitHub Actions.

notes.front: You automate setting an organisation’s artifact and log retention to 30 days. Which call do you make?
notes.back: `PUT /orgs/{org}/actions/permissions/artifact-and-log-retention` with `days` set to 30.
notes.explanation: OAuth app tokens and personal access tokens (classic) need the `admin:org` scope or the “Actions policies” fine-grained permission, because the call changes an organisation policy.
notes.source: GitHub Docs, “REST API endpoints for GitHub Actions permissions”, “Set artifact and log retention settings for an organization”
notes.evidence: PUT /orgs/{org}/actions/permissions/artifact-and-log-retention ``` Sets artifact and log retention settings for an organization. OAuth app tokens and personal access tokens (classic) need the admin:org scope or the "Actions policies" fine-grained permission to use this endpoint.

notes.front: An auditor asks you to keep a private repository’s workflow logs for one year. What do you do?
notes.choices:
A) Nothing is possible: the maximum is 90 days
B) Set its retention period to 365 days
C) Ask GitHub Support to raise the limit
D) Make the repository public, which allows longer retention
notes.back: B) Set its retention period to 365 days
notes.choicesExplained: A: 90 days is the cap for public repositories only. C: 365 days is already within the private range. D: public repositories have the lower cap.
notes.explanation: Private repositories accept any period from 1 to 400 days.
notes.source: GitHub Docs, “Configuring the retention period for checks, workflow runs, commit statuses, artifacts, and logs in your organization”, “Configuring the retention period for checks, workflow runs, commit statuses, artifacts, and logs in your organization”
notes.evidence: For private repositories: you can change this retention period to anywhere between 1 day or 400 days.

notes.front: What does the Access setting in a private repository’s Actions settings control?
notes.back: Whether workflows in the same owner’s other private repositories can use its actions and reusable workflows.
notes.explanation: Sharing is limited to other private repositories with the same owner.
notes.source: GitHub Docs, “Managing GitHub Actions settings for a repository”, “Allowing access to components in a private repository”
notes.evidence: Actions and reusable workflows in your private repositories can be shared with other private repositories owned by the same user or organization.

notes.front: Workflows in your organisation’s private repositories cannot use a composite action kept in another private repository of the same organisation. What do you change?
notes.choices:
A) Set that repository’s Access to allow repositories in the organisation
B) Make the action’s repository public
C) Add the action to the enterprise allow list with `!`
D) Move the action into a `.github` repository
notes.back: A) Set that repository’s Access to allow repositories in the organisation
notes.choicesExplained: B: not needed; private repositories can share with other private repositories of the same owner. C: `!` blocks an entry. D: the `.github` repository holds templates, and access would still be needed.
notes.explanation: The Access setting lets other private repositories in the organisation use its actions and reusable workflows.
notes.source: GitHub Docs, “Managing GitHub Actions settings for a repository”, “Managing access for a private repository in an organization”
notes.evidence: Workflows in other repositories that are part of the 'ORGANIZATION NAME' organization can access the actions and reusable workflows in this repository. Access is allowed only from private repositories.

notes.front: A repository admin cannot change the repository’s Actions permissions. What is a likely cause?
notes.back: An overriding policy from the organisation or its enterprise.
notes.explanation: Repository settings sit beneath organisation and enterprise policy.
notes.source: GitHub Docs, “Managing GitHub Actions settings for a repository”, “Managing GitHub Actions permissions for your repository”
notes.evidence: You might not be able to manage these settings if your organization has an overriding policy or is managed by an enterprise that has overriding policy.

notes.front: For organisation cache settings, what are the default and the maximum cache retention?
notes.back: 7 days by default; up to 365 days, or the enterprise’s limit.
notes.explanation: An organisation owned by an enterprise cannot go above the enterprise’s limit.
notes.source: GitHub Docs, “Disabling or limiting GitHub Actions for your organization”, “Configuring GitHub Actions cache settings for your organization”
notes.evidence: Cache retention**: The maximum number of days to retain caches before automatic deletion. The default is 7 days. You can configure up to 365 days (or up to the limit set by your enterprise).

notes.front: How does allowing only your organisation’s actions differ from “Allow owner, and select non-owner, actions and reusable workflows”?
notes.back: The first blocks every outside action, even GitHub’s; the second adds chosen outside ones.
notes.explanation: Under the select option, actions within the organisation are allowed and further options admit specific outside ones.
notes.source: GitHub Docs, “Disabling or limiting GitHub Actions for your organization”, “Managing GitHub Actions permissions for your organization”
notes.evidence: If you choose **Allow *OWNER*, and select non-*OWNER*, actions and reusable workflows**, actions and reusable workflows within your organization are allowed, and there are additional options for allowing other specific actions and reusable workflows.
